title: What is AGILE and what is SDLC, and how do they differ?
shortTitle: What AGILE and SDLC are, and how they differ
topicTitle: What is AGILE and what is SDLC

s1_definition.profdef: SDLC, the Software Development Life Cycle, is the overall framework of phases a software product passes through from conception to retirement — typically requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance. It describes what work must happen, not how often or in what cadence. Agile is a set of values and principles, defined by the Agile Manifesto, for how to run that life cycle: iteratively and incrementally, in short cycles that deliver working software frequently, welcome changing requirements, and favour close collaboration and feedback over heavy up-front planning. The key distinction is that SDLC is the what — the phases — while Agile is a how — one philosophy of sequencing and executing those phases, in contrast to alternatives like the Waterfall model which runs the same phases once, sequentially, start to finish.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of building National Bank of India's new mobile app. SDLC is the list of stages any construction must go through: figure out what to build, design it, build it, test it, open it to customers, and maintain it. Agile and Waterfall are two different ways to march through those stages. Waterfall is like constructing the entire building in one long sequence — finish all the planning, then all the building, then hand over the keys once at the end. Agile is like building and opening one floor at a time, getting customers to use each floor and give feedback before you build the next, so you can change the design as you learn.
s1_definition.oneliner: SDLC is the set of phases every project goes through; Agile is a way of moving through those phases in short, feedback-driven iterations rather than one big sequential pass.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** SDLC, the Software Development Life Cycle, is the overall framework of phases a software product passes through from conception to retirement — typically requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance. It describes what work must happen, not how often or in what cadence. Agile is a set of values and principles, defined by the Agile Manifesto, for how to run that life cycle: iteratively and incrementally, in short cycles that deliver working software frequently, welcome changing requirements, and favour close collaboration and feedback over heavy up-front planning. The key distinction is that SDLC is the what — the phases — while Agile is a how — one philosophy of sequencing and executing those phases, in contrast to alternatives like the Waterfall model which runs the same phases once, sequentially, start to finish.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of building National Bank of India's new mobile app. SDLC is the list of stages any construction must go through: figure out what to build, design it, build it, test it, open it to customers, and maintain it. Agile and Waterfall are two different ways to march through those stages. Waterfall is like constructing the entire building in one long sequence — finish all the planning, then all the building, then hand over the keys once at the end. Agile is like building and opening one floor at a time, getting customers to use each floor and give feedback before you build the next, so you can change the design as you learn.

**One line to remember:** SDLC is the set of phases every project goes through; Agile is a way of moving through those phases in short, feedback-driven iterations rather than one big sequential pass.

sections.s2_technical:
SDLC names the fundamental phases that any software effort involves, regardless of methodology. In the requirements phase you gather and agree what the system must do. In the design phase you decide the architecture, the data model, and the interfaces. In the implementation phase you write the code. In the testing phase you verify the software meets the requirements and is free of serious defects. In deployment you release it to users. In maintenance you fix issues, adapt to change, and eventually retire the system. Every real project touches these activities; SDLC is simply the vocabulary and structure for them. Crucially, SDLC does not dictate how often you cycle through the phases or how much you do at once — that is a separate choice of model.

The model you lay over SDLC determines the rhythm. The classic Waterfall model runs the phases exactly once in a strict sequence: you complete all requirements, then all design, then all implementation, then all testing, then release. It assumes requirements are known up front and stable. Its strength is predictability and heavy documentation, which some regulated contexts like. Its weakness is that it discovers problems late — you do not see working software until near the end — and it handles change poorly, because a requirement discovered during testing means revisiting earlier phases expensively.

Agile overlays the same phases but runs them in many short iterations. Rather than designing everything then building everything, an Agile team takes a small slice of functionality, carries it through requirements, design, build, and test within a short iteration, and delivers working software at the end of that iteration. Then it repeats. This is the heart of being iterative and incremental: each iteration produces a potentially shippable increment, and the product grows slice by slice. The Agile Manifesto captures the values behind this: individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, and responding to change over following a plan. It does not say the right-hand items have no value; it says the left-hand items are valued more.

Agile is a mindset, and specific frameworks implement it. Scrum organizes work into fixed-length iterations called sprints, usually two weeks, with defined roles such as the Product Owner who prioritizes the backlog and the Scrum Master who facilitates, and ceremonies such as sprint planning, the daily stand-up, the sprint review where the increment is demonstrated, and the retrospective where the team improves its process. Kanban instead focuses on a continuous flow of work visualized on a board with limits on how much work is in progress at once, pulling new work only as capacity frees up. Both are Agile; they differ in how they structure the flow.

The practical differences between Agile and Waterfall matter day to day. Agile delivers value early and often, so stakeholders see working software within weeks and can course-correct. It welcomes changing requirements even late, because the next iteration can absorb them. It surfaces risk early, because integration and testing happen every iteration rather than being deferred. Waterfall, by contrast, offers a fixed scope and timeline that some fixed-price contracts or heavily regulated deliverables prefer, but pays for that with late feedback and costly change.

The senior-level nuance is that Agile and SDLC are not competitors and the question's framing can mislead a junior. SDLC is the container; Agile is one way to fill it. In a modern banking environment Agile is almost always combined with engineering practices that make frequent delivery safe: continuous integration so every change is built and tested automatically, continuous delivery so increments can be released on demand, automated testing so quality does not regress with speed, and DevOps collaboration so the same team that builds also operates. Agile without these practices degrades into chaotic frequent change; with them, it delivers the responsiveness the manifesto promises. It is also worth being honest in an interview that pure Waterfall still appears where requirements are genuinely fixed and change is costly, and that many organizations run a hybrid, using Agile iterations for build while keeping some up-front architecture and compliance gates that a regulated bank requires.
sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, two teams are building the same feature — a new loan-application flow — one using a Waterfall approach and one using Agile, and leadership wants to compare how quickly working software and feedback arrive.

Problem 1 — The Waterfall team completes all requirements, then all design, then all build, then all test, and only releases at the very end. If a requirement was misunderstood, nobody finds out until testing, which is late and expensive. This is exactly the late-feedback weakness of running SDLC phases once sequentially.

Problem 2 — The Agile team takes the loan flow one slice at a time — first a basic application form, then credit checks, then document upload — carrying each slice through all phases within a two-week sprint and demoing it. Feedback arrives every sprint. This is exactly the iterative, incremental strength of Agile.

Problem 3 — Leadership wants to see, concretely, when working software first appears and how a mid-project requirement change is absorbed under each approach. This is exactly the comparison the demo will make visible.

To make this runnable, we will build a small program that models both approaches over the same SDLC phases. It will contain an `SdlcPhase` enum, a `Methodology` interface with `Waterfall` and `Agile` implementations, and a `DeliveryTracker` that records when working software is first delivered and how a requirement change introduced partway through is handled. The demo runs the same loan feature through both, printing the week each produces usable software and how each responds to a change, so the difference between the two ways of traversing SDLC is unmistakable.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the same loan-application feature, split into four slices, run once through Waterfall and once through Agile, with a requirement change introduced partway through each.

Step 1: The Waterfall run begins. It takes the whole feature through each SDLC phase in sequence — requirements, then design, then implementation, then testing — each consuming about two weeks. No working software exists during any of these phases because everything is being done at once for the entire feature.

Step 2: Only after the deployment phase, around week ten in this model, does Waterfall produce working software. The tracker records that first delivery week. This illustrates the defining Waterfall trait: value appears late, in one lump at the end.

Step 3: A requirement change is discovered at week seven, during Waterfall's testing. Because the design and implementation phases are already complete, absorbing the change means reopening those finished phases, which the tracker records as a high-cost change. This is the costly-late-change weakness.

Step 4: The Agile run begins. It takes the first slice, the application form, through all the SDLC phases within a single two-week sprint, and delivers it as a shippable increment at week two. The tracker records that as the first delivery — working software exists within two weeks, not ten.

Step 5: Agile continues slice by slice — credit check, document upload, approval — each a sprint that again touches all phases for just that slice and ends in a demo. The product grows incrementally, and stakeholders give feedback every sprint.

Step 6: A requirement change arrives at week five, mid-project. In Agile it simply becomes a backlog item that the next sprint absorbs, which the tracker records as a low-cost change. The final summary shows Waterfall first delivering around week ten with high change cost, and Agile first delivering at week two with low change cost, making the difference between the two traversals of the identical SDLC phases concrete.

sections.s6_takeaway:
SDLC, the Software Development Life Cycle, is the overall framework of phases every software product passes through: requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance. It describes what work must happen, but it does not say how often you cycle through those phases or how much you tackle at once. Agile is different in kind — it is a set of values and principles from the Agile Manifesto for how to run the life cycle, specifically iteratively and incrementally, delivering working software in short cycles, welcoming change, and favouring collaboration and feedback over heavy up-front planning. So the clean way I put it in an interview is that SDLC is the what — the phases — and Agile is a how — one philosophy for sequencing and executing those phases.

The contrast is sharpest against Waterfall, which is the other main way to traverse SDLC. Waterfall runs the phases exactly once in strict sequence: all requirements, then all design, then all build, then all test, then release. It assumes requirements are known and stable up front. Its strengths are predictability and documentation, which some regulated or fixed-price contexts value, but its weaknesses are that it discovers problems late, because you do not see working software until near the end, and it handles change poorly, because a requirement found during testing means reopening completed phases at high cost. Agile overlays the same phases but runs them in many short iterations, taking one slice of functionality through requirements, design, build, and test within a sprint and delivering a shippable increment, then repeating. Value arrives early and often, risk surfaces every iteration, and late changes are simply absorbed into the next sprint.

Agile is a mindset implemented by frameworks. Scrum uses fixed two-week sprints with roles like the Product Owner and Scrum Master and ceremonies like planning, the daily stand-up, the review, and the retrospective. Kanban uses a continuous flow with limits on work in progress, pulling new work as capacity frees. Both are Agile; they differ in how they structure the flow.

The judgement I bring is that Agile and SDLC are not competitors — SDLC is the container and Agile is one way to fill it. At National Bank of India, Agile only worked because it was paired with the engineering practices that make frequent delivery safe: continuous integration so every change is built and tested automatically, continuous delivery so increments can be released on demand, automated testing so quality does not regress with speed, and close DevOps collaboration. Agile without those degrades into chaotic change; with them it delivers the responsiveness the manifesto promises. I am also honest that pure Waterfall still fits where requirements are genuinely fixed, and that a regulated bank often runs a hybrid — Agile iterations for the build, with some deliberate up-front architecture and compliance gates that the regulator requires.
